analysis.one_liner: Bars lawsuits blaming food companies for obesity and weight-related health problems.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban lawsuits against food makers and sellers over obesity-related claims, with 16 Senate cosponsors including 4 Democrats, died in the Judiciary Committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to file any new federal or state lawsuit against food manufacturers, marketers, distributors, advertisers, sellers, or their trade associations seeking damages for a person's weight gain, obesity, or related health conditions, and would have required courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuits already pending [S2][S3]. It kept narrow exceptions: lawsuits over a broken express contract or warranty, lawsuits alleging a company knowingly violated advertising or labeling law and someone relied on that violation, and enforcement cases brought by the FTC or FDA [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, food and beverage manufacturers, restaurant chains, food marketers and advertisers, and their trade associations would have gained permanent immunity from obesity-related tort claims, including suits already on file, which would have been dismissed immediately [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food makers, sellers, advertisers, trade associations

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any new civil action, in federal or state court, against food manufacturers, marketers, distributors, advertisers, sellers, or trade associations for damages or relief arising out of a person's accumulated consumption of food and resulting weight gain, obesity, or related health conditions [S2][S3].
Requires courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuit already pending on the date of enactment, taking away recourse from people whose cases were already filed [S3].

Stays discovery in covered cases filed after May 7, 2007 while a motion to dismiss under the bill is decided, keeping documents and internal company information out of plaintiffs' hands during that period [S3].

Leaves narrower paths open: claims for breach of an express contract or warranty unrelated to weight gain, claims that a company knowingly violated advertising or labeling law with intent that consumers rely on the violation, and enforcement actions by the FTC and FDA [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, consumers who were injured or misled would have lost a legal avenue to hold food sellers accountable in court, and any public costs of treating obesity-related disease would have stayed with taxpayers rather than being shifted toward companies through litigation. The bill's own findings argue these lawsuits are frivolous and would raise costs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and injured patients suing food sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill would have erased plaintiffs' right to sue even in cases where discovery might have revealed deceptive marketing practices, since covered claims would be dismissed outright and discovery frozen while dismissal motions were pending [S3].

Supporters argued the opposite case in the bill's own findings: weight gain and obesity result from many factors, including genetics and personal choices, so blaming any single food or seller is unfair, legally frivolous, and economically damaging, and lawsuits would raise costs for everyone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered the food industry a sweeping liability shield covering even pending lawsuits, while leaving government agencies, not injured individuals, as the main check on deceptive food marketing. Whether that trade-off is acceptable depends on how much weight one gives the argument that obesity suits are meritless personal-responsibility theater versus the argument that the threat of lawsuits is one of the few tools individuals have against large companies. As written, the industry got nearly everything and consumers lost nearly everything, so the design favored the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the bill on May 7, 2007, joined by eight original cosponsors including Democrats Mark Pryor, Blanche Lincoln, and Max Baucus [S3][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was recorded for the rest of the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill gathered 16 cosponsors in total, 12 Republicans and 4 Democrats, but never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any House action [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers who might have sued food companies came out ahead, because they kept the right to file obesity-related liability claims; the food and beverage industry did not get the immunity it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers kept the right to sue food sellers

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers and sellers
industries.note: The bill would have handed them blanket immunity from obesity-related lawsuits, including suits already in court, and frozen discovery that could expose internal documents. Consumers would have borne the cost of losing that legal recourse.
As sellers and marketers of food, restaurants were squarely covered by the lawsuit ban; the bill was aimed at the wave of obesity suits against fast-food chains.
Trade associations of food companies were named as protected defendants in the bill, extending the shield beyond the companies themselves.
Advertisers and marketers of food were covered defendants; the narrow exception for knowing violations of advertising law was the only path left for consumers misled by marketing.
The bill would have wiped out this category of consumer litigation, including pending cases; their loss tracked directly with consumers' loss of recourse.
